newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. chief applauds Italian-led Albania force.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief applauds Italian-led Albania force.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Tuesday applauded the efforts of an Italian-led multinational force to Albania but stressed that the goals of the mission should remain humanitarian.

"I think the concept of the mission...has the right approach to make sure that food gets into the hands of needy and not into the hands of outlaws," Annan told reporters after talks with Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Annan, on a visit to Italy and the Vatican, was briefed by the Italian military on the strategy for the 6,000-strong force which began deploying on Tuesday to protect aid convoys to the impoverished Balkan state.

Nearly 300 people have died in Albania, Europe's poorest state, after rebels looted tens of thousands of weapons from state armouries following the collapse of dubious get-rich-quick savings schemes earlier this year.
Annan said however that the multinational force, which has the backing of the U.N. Security Council, had no mandate to disarm rebels and this should be done by the Albanian people themselves.

"Disarmament is a very tricky issue and should be an (Albanian) national effort...possibly the government could buy back the weapons," he said. "This operation is a humanitarian one to make sure aid gets to the people."

Prodi said the force would also have as its priority the smooth running of new general elections called by President Sali Berisha for June after rebels demanded his resignation over the savings fiasco.
"Election and aid are the two issues of our mission," Prodi said.
More than 1,000 Italian, French and Spanish troops landed by air and sea on Tuesday to spearhead the force which is to aid distribution of food and medical supplies to violence-swept Albania.
Troops from Austria, Denmark, Romania, Greece and Turkey are also taking part.
Prodi has said Italy could start bringing troops back a month after the elections but they may have to stay for up to a maximum of six months.
